column1: # @ROOT@ is substituted with the git-sandbox root at run time and @NL@ with a
# newline (a heredoc-bearing command is multi-line, and a cell cannot hold one).
# Every generic rule (guard-kit/SPEC.md §The generic ruleset) has a firing + a
# non-firing case. Columns are tab-separated; # and blank lines are ignored.
# rule 1 — cd in a compound command
# rule 2 — a prefix spelling that falls off the match path: (a) git -C <repo-root>
#          when cwd is the root, (b) a git -c config override among git's global
#          options, (c) an absolute spelling of a wrapper the matcher strips. A
#          quoted mention and a wrapper path in argument position are not the command
# rule 4 — absolute-path read-only repo script (rewrite) vs other script (block).
#          The rewrite emits allow, so it attaches only when the rewritten command
#          is allowlisted (the sandbox carries both script globs) and stays inside
#          rule 24's path slots; otherwise the corrective block fires, for an
#          unallowlisted scratch script and for a runner glob reached past its slot
# rule 5 — repo-root absolute prefix (non-script) steered; foreign path untouched.
#          The rule declares 'sq dq hd', so a path merely *named* — quoted either
#          way, or sitting in a heredoc body — is not the executable command.
#          The heredoc row lands on `allow` rather than `fallthrough` because
#          rule 17's create grant reaches it fourteen rules later; a rule-5
#          regression would still read `block`, which is what this row asserts.
# rule 6 — shell expansion / assignment; single-quoted $ stays literal.
#          'sq' only: a double-quoted "$x" expands, and so does an
#          unquoted-delimiter heredoc body — the stated bound on the hd class.
# 'hdq': an unquoted delimiter expands, so its body stays live; a quoted one
# cannot expand, and the shell is what guarantees that — so its body is inert
# reaches rule 21's advisory, which is the correct verdict for a commit -F; the
# point is that rule 6 no longer blocks it before rule 21 is ever consulted

column2: git commit -F - <<'MSG'@NL@names a $(cmd) in the body@NL@MSG

column1: # rule 7 — unquoted brace glyph: bare {} placeholder rewritten, expansions blocked.
#          'sq dq hd': '{' is a matcher glyph, not an expansion, so a
#          double-quoted quantifier and a heredoc-body brace are both inert —
#          the corrective (spell the members) is inapplicable to either.
#          The placeholder rewrite emits allow, so it attaches only when the
#          rewritten command is allowlisted and stays inside rule 24's path slots;
#          an unallowlisted and an unbounded placeholder block with the quoted-
# rule 8 — sed or awk reading a file, or sed rewriting one; a piped-into sed is a
#          filter. awk fires on two read shapes, each with one file operand and no
#          pipe into the segment — a line range (steered to Read) and a markdown
#          heading range (steered to the section extractor); a transform, a
#          single-regex filter, a program file, a non-.md range, a second operand
#          and a piped-into awk all pass
# rule 9 — listing-only find steered to Glob, alone or as a ';'-batch of listings
#          (a literal banner between them is fine); action-predicate / piped /

column2: find lib -type f; find lib -type d
find lib -type f; echo ===; find lib -type d

column1: # rule 10 — bare single-file cat steered to Read, alone or as a ';'-batch of reads
#           (a literal echo/printf banner between reads is fine); multi-file, piped,
#           redirected, &&-chained, mixed, and banner-only forms are composition and pass
# rule 11 — working-tree git grep steered to Grep (a path-limited `-- <path>`
#           search is still the working tree); a revision or --cached passes
# rule 12 — self-matching process-liveness predicate: a `pgrep -f` pattern the
#           command's own text repeats can never go false, since `-f` scans the
#           waiter's own argv. A lone query, a `pgrep` without `-f`, and a pattern
#           occurring nowhere else are genuine queries and pass.

column2: bash run-smoke.sh & until ! pgrep -f run-smoke.sh; do sleep 5; done

column1: # rule 13 — bare foreground sleep steered to a condition wait. The non-firing
#           cases are the load-bearing ones: a sleep inside an `until … do … done`
#           loop *is* the sanctioned form, and a quoted mention is inert. Both
#           are `allow` rather than `fallthrough` because a later auto-allow
#           grants them outright — rule 17 the append, rule 19 the wait — and
#           each still proves rule 13 inert, since a block exits 2 at rule 13 and
#           never reaches an auto-allow six rules later.

column2: until grep -q DONE .tmp/smoke.log; do sleep 5; done

column1: # rule 14 — tracked-tree mutation under a live producer. The sandbox's only
#           `*.run` record names a dead pid and a non-record file sits beside
#           it, so every mutating form below declines: the rule's second
#           conjunct is a *live* record, and read-only git never reaches it at
#           all. The block arm needs a pid the test owns and lives in
# rule 15 — a backgrounded launch that records no producer is blocked. The
#           shell `&` arm lives here because it *is* command text; the harness
#           flag is tool input and cannot be written in this grammar, so that
# exemption (3) reads rule 18's declared forms: a backgrounded pipeline writing
# through a member's own option owns work a commit could corrupt
# rule 16 — `: > file` truncation auto-allowed iff every target is gitignored
# rule 17 — a write to gitignored targets auto-allowed, create and append alike.
#           The clauses each get their refusing case, because each is what keeps
#           the grant from blessing something the redirect alone would: (b) a
#           target outside the ignore set, (c) a leading command that writes
#           somewhere other than its stdout, and the single-statement half of
#           (c) — a second statement on a line of its own, which is what the
#           heredoc residue must never be confused with.
#           Targets are relative, as rules 3 and 16's are: the runner drives the
#           guard from inside the sandbox, and an `@ROOT@`-absolute target would
#           meet rule 5's repo-root-prefix block nine rules earlier.
# (d)'s region test is `hdq`, not the raw command: a backtick in a QUOTED
# delimiter's body cannot substitute, so the grant reaches the shape the mandated
# journal append is always spelled in; an UNQUOTED delimiter leaves the body live
# and the decline still fires. Nothing else distinguishes the two at the grant
# boundary, so these two rows are the whole holder of the asymmetry.
# the create half rests on rule 16: `: > f` and then `cat >> f` are each already
# granted, so a create adds one permission decision and no capability. Every
# other clause still holds — a tracked target refuses on the per-target ignore
# test the append case takes, which is the row that would catch an over-wide grant
# the two inert targets are exempt from (a) and (b): neither is a file the
# append-only split protects, and neither is a path git check-ignore can answer
# rule 18 — read-only pipeline auto-allow; a non-roster segment falls through
# banner tolerance (rules 9 and 10's, third caller): a literal echo/printf
# segment is skipped, but at least one roster read must remain
# widened lead: a bare committed allow entry may lead, since it was reviewed —
# but only where something decorates it, so the undecorated form (rule 20's
# 'fallthrough git status' below) is still never intercepted here
# xargs is on the roster but executes rather than filters, so it is granted only
# when the command it runs is itself a roster binary. The refusing cases are the
# point of the discriminator: each is a write, and each is silently granted

column2: grep -rln foo src | xargs sed -i s/a/b/

column1: # declared forms: a roster member is read-only only in none of its declared write
# and execute forms (the kit's table here; a consumer's entries are the knob
# test's lane). Each refusing row is a write the leads-with test alone granted:
# an option in its long, abbreviated, clustered and quoted spellings, uniq's output
# positional, find's write predicates, rg's preprocessor, and the command xargs runs
# rule 19 — a sanctioned wait auto-allowed. Arm (A), the bounded in-turn wait: the
#           grant rows are the two of the four measured calls it is shaped to
#           cover, both compounds; the refusing rows are one per clause, so no
#           clause can be deleted without a red. The two named non-targets (`pgrep`
#           and `gh` as conditions) are clause (c)'s refusals and are declined on
#           purpose. Arm (B), the recorded launch, follows arm (A)'s rows.

column2: until grep -q DONE .tmp/smoke.log; do sleep 20; done; echo waited
until grep -q DONE .tmp/smoke.log 2>/dev/null; do sleep 30; done; grep -n ERR .tmp/smoke.log

column1: # the literal-PID liveness wait rule 13's corrective now spells, in both
# polarities — the form the ruleset steers toward, granted rather than prompted
# clause (0) — a statement-ending `&` is a launch, not a wait, whatever else the
# command does. Rule 15 exempts the wait loop, so this row reaches rule 19 and
# is refused there rather than by an earlier rule's ordering

column2: until grep -q DONE .tmp/smoke.log; do sleep 5; done &

column1: # clause (a) — the first statement is not the loop

column2: echo start; until grep -q DONE .tmp/smoke.log; do sleep 5; done

column1: # clause (b) — the body runs something besides sleep

column2: until grep -q DONE .tmp/smoke.log; do grep -c x .tmp/smoke.log; sleep 5; done

column1: # clause (c) — the two stated non-targets: a pattern match where a PID belongs,
# and a network tool that already has a blocking primitive

column2: while pgrep -f worker >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 20; done; echo waited
until gh run view 12 --json status 2>/dev/null | grep -q completed; do sleep 30; done

column1: # clause (d) — a tail statement rule 18 would not have granted standing alone

column2: until grep -q DONE .tmp/smoke.log; do sleep 5; done; git commit -m done

column1: # clause (e) — a backtick anywhere in the raw command; the `$(…)` spelling is
# deliberately not a row, since rule 6 blocks it first and the row would pin

column2: until grep -q DONE `cat .tmp/f`; do sleep 5; done

column1: # a non-inert redirect on the loop itself is a write, and a grant may not bless one

column2: until grep -q DONE .tmp/smoke.log; do sleep 5; done > out.txt

column1: # clauses (c) and (d) take rule 18's declared forms over the whole call, so a
# condition or a tail writing through a roster member's own option is refused

column2: while sort -c -o out.txt data.txt; do sleep 5; done
until grep -q DONE .tmp/smoke.log; do sleep 5; done; sort -o out.txt .tmp/smoke.log

column1: # arm (B) — the launch-record-wait spelling rule 15's corrective names, granted for an
# allowlisted, bounded launch writing only gitignored targets, with and without the

column2: bash scripts/check-foo.sh > .tmp/foo.log 2>&1 & echo "pid=$! run=foo" > .tmp/foo.run; wait; rm -f .tmp/foo.run

column1: # (B0) the shape: a record whose filename does not carry its key, and no wait
# (B1) a launch the allowlist does not grant reaches the harness's own decision

column2: bash worker.sh > .tmp/worker.log 2>&1 & echo "pid=$! run=worker" > .tmp/worker.run; wait; rm -f .tmp/worker.run

column1: # (B1) granted launches the later rules refuse, each taken as a predicate: a runner
# glob reached past its slot (rule 24, which cannot decide the whole call and
# declines), a scratch script body (rule 23) and a forced git rm (rule 22), the last
# two then blocked at their own rule

column2: git rm -q -f tracked.md & echo "pid=$! run=x" > .tmp/x.run; wait

column1: # (B2) a launch writing a tracked target, through every redirect operator that writes one

column2: bash scripts/check-foo.sh > tracked.md & echo "pid=$! run=foo" > .tmp/foo.run; wait
bash scripts/check-foo.sh &> tracked.md & echo "pid=$! run=foo" > .tmp/foo.run; wait
bash scripts/check-foo.sh &>> tracked.md & echo "pid=$! run=foo" > .tmp/foo.run; wait
bash scripts/check-foo.sh <> tracked.md & echo "pid=$! run=foo" > .tmp/foo.run; wait

column1: # (B3) an expansion besides the record's own; rule 24's predicate declines a live '$'
# in the launch too, so this row pins the verdict rather than the clause alone
# rule 20 — decorated allowlisted bare lead with an unmatched segment blocked;
#           chaining steer, redirect steer, and the untouched non-firing cases
# rule 21 — git history-rewrite advisory: amend / commit -F / soft-reset steered;
#           a plain commit and a non-soft reset pass
# rule 22 — bare rm of a tracked path steers to 'git rm -q'; untracked,
#           gitignored, and the already-correct git rm form pass
# rule 22's force arm — a 'git rm' carrying its force flag is blocked whether or
#           not a grant matches: standalone, in a short cluster, long, abbreviated
#           as git's option parser accepts it, behind a global option, and quoted.
#           A word after '--' is a path, and '--cached' keeps the file
# rule 23 — a script interpreter taking its program body from a scratch dir.
#           The firing rows are delta 3's probe table promoted from evidence into
#           fixtures: one per body source, both arms. Targets are relative, as
#           rules 3, 16 and 17's are — an `@ROOT@`-absolute one would meet rule 5
# arm (a), bash/sh: the operand form is the steer this rule inherited from a
#          consumer rule, and the stdin form is the widening the re-key buys it
# arm (b), one row per body source: operand, stdin redirect with and without the
# '-', the device-path spelling of the same redirect, and the pipe producer
# the backtick substitution — the one spelling rule 6 does not reach, which makes
# it the case whose absence would leave a silently teachable spelling. The '$(…)'
# spelling is deliberately NOT a case: rule 6 blocks it first, so a row here would
# pin another rule's verdict and go green for the wrong reason the day rule 6 changed
# falls through — the body rides in the command string, so the approver and the
# friction log both see it verbatim and there is nothing to compensate for. This
# is the boundary most likely to regress silently, so it carries the most cases
# falls through — outside the scratch scope: a tracked tool's body is reviewable
# in the repo, and the runner's own invocation takes a scratch path as an
# argument to a tracked script rather than as a body
# rule 24 — a committed grant matched only by reaching past its path slot. The
#           sandbox carries a scratch 'rm -rf .tmp/*' grant and a
#           '*/checks/check-*.sh' runner glob: a '..' component, an absolute path,
#           a second operand outside the slot and a reach behind a stripped wrapper
#           each block, while a clean slot, a dropped redirect and a declined
#           backtick fall through. Targets are untracked, so rule 22 never answers
# rule 25 — anything else falls through to the friction log
